pages.spec: Know what you will study in KS3 ICT and how the department expects you to work
pages.summary: KS3 ICT teaches you what goes on behind the scenes of a computer and how to program one. Work and homework are shared on Google Classroom, and if you miss a lesson it is your job to catch up.

blocks.text: Welcome to the ICT department at Enniskillen Royal Grammar School! **[[ICT]]** stands for **Information and Communications Technology**. It is about how computers and other digital devices store, process and share information.

You will learn far more than how to switch on a games console or use an app on your phone. You will find out what actually goes on *behind the scenes* of a computer, and you will learn to write your own code. ERGS is a programming school, so by the end of KS3 you will have the skills to start building your own games, websites and apps.
*"You don't have to be great to start, but you have to start to be great."* Everyone starts at the beginning, so don't worry if some of your friends have used computers more than you.

blocks.text: Google Classroom and MySchool

[[MySchool]] is the website you log in to with your school username and password. From it you can reach your school email and other tools. Your teacher (Mr Butler) uploads lessons, handouts and homework to **[[Google Classroom]]**. Every subject uses Google Classroom, and so do many school clubs and teams, so it is worth learning to use it well now. Take a note of your teacher's email address too, in case you cannot get into the resources.
If you are absent from class
If you miss an ICT lesson for any reason, it is **your responsibility** to catch up before the next lesson. That means:

items: Check whether any homework is due, and complete it.
Catch up on any work or notes you missed. If you don't understand them, see your teacher before the next lesson.
If there was a class test, see your teacher before the next lesson so you can sit it, or so a time can be arranged.

blocks.text: "I wasn't here last lesson" is **not** accepted as an excuse for missing homework. Ask a classmate, check Google Classroom or email your teacher.
If you know you will be absent (for example, for a school trip or a match), tell your teacher beforehand. You may be able to do the work early.

At the start of Year 8 you fill in a **Pupil Baseline Survey**. It is not a test. It simply tells your teacher what computer equipment you can use at home, so they can spot any problems early. Fill it in honestly using your c2k email address.

Lessons, handouts and homework are posted on Google Classroom.

pages.spec: Know the school's Acceptable Use Policy and the top 10 rules of the computer room
pages.summary: Everyone must use the school network for learning and act responsibly. The Acceptable Use Policy and the top 10 computer room rules explain what is and is not allowed.

blocks.text: The school network is for your **education**. Every user is expected to act responsibly and to show consideration to others. Using the school's computers for anything that is not educational will bring about **[[sanction|sanctions]]** (punishments), and attempts to reach blocked sites are recorded on your account.
The Acceptable Use Policy

An **[[Acceptable Use Policy]]** (AUP) is a set of rules you agree to before you are allowed to use the computers. It keeps **you** safe and it keeps the **network and its data** safe. Before you can use a school computer you sign the **School Computer Contract**, which is your promise to follow these rules.

items: **Never** tell anyone your password.
Only log on to **your own** account, and **log off** when you leave a [[workstation]].
Do not download, store or install software on school computers.
Do not try to introduce a virus or any malicious (harmful) code to the network.
Do not access, download, create, store or send material that is indecent or obscene, or that brings the name of the school into disrepute (gives it a bad name).
Do not use public chat rooms or social networks in school.
Do not directly copy material from the internet and use it as your own work.

Logging in as a friend, even "for a laugh", breaks the rules. Anything done on that account looks like it was done by your friend.

pages.spec: Explain what a computer, a network and the internet are
pages.summary: A computer is a machine that stores and processes data by following instructions. A network is two or more computers joined so they can communicate and share. The internet is the biggest network of all, and nobody owns it.

blocks.text: What is a computer?

A **[[computer]]** is a type of machine. It is used for storing and processing **[[data]]** by following instructions given to it in a **program**. Because the program can be changed, the same computer can do lots of different jobs: a word processor one minute, a game the next.
A computer doesn't have a brain like a human, so it can't think or have ideas of its own. It only does exactly what its instructions tell it to, but it does that very fast and very accurately.
What is a network?

A **[[network]]** is made when **two or more computers are joined together**. This means they can communicate with each other and share things like **printers** and **files**. A single computer that doesn't share or send data with any other computer is not a network.

items: **The internet**: the biggest network in the world.
**Home WiFi**: your phone, laptop, console and smart TV all joined to your router.
**Gaming networks**: such as PlayStation Network or Xbox network, letting you play friends online.
**Social networks**: such as Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok or YouTube, which join people together online.

blocks.text: The internet

The **[[internet]]** is a **worldwide network**. It lets computers from all over the world communicate with each other, for example to send email, play online games and use social networks. A pupil in Enniskillen can play a game against someone in Australia because both consoles are connected to the internet.
Who owns the internet?
**Nobody** is in charge of the whole internet. This means almost anybody can put almost anything onto it, which can cause problems because offensive or untrue material can appear.
You are not invisible online. Every device connected to the internet has an address (an **IP address**), so the police can often trace who posted something, even from a fake account.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A computer stores and processes data by following a program; it cannot think for itself.
A network = two or more computers joined together to communicate and share.
Examples of networks: the internet, home WiFi, gaming networks, social networks.
The internet is a worldwide network; nobody owns or controls all of it.

pages.spec: Describe the school network, why you need a unique login and how to set a strong password
pages.summary: School workstations are controlled by a server on the C2k network. You log in with a unique User ID and a secret password, which should be strong: at least 8 characters mixing capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols.

blocks.text: The school network

All the computers on the school network are controlled by a main computer called a **[[server]]**. The server lets everyone save their files **centrally** (in one place, so you can reach them from any computer in school) and share things like **printers**. The computer you sit at and use is called a **[[workstation]]**.
In some networks there is a **switch** or **hub** in the centre that the workstations plug into. For now, we will always label the centre of a network diagram as the server.
Logging in
Every pupil can use the school network. It is called the **[[C2k]]** network, and it runs in schools throughout Northern Ireland. You have login details to tell the server who you are:

items: A **[[User ID]]**: this is **unique**, so no one else has the same one. It tells the server *who* you are.
A **[[password]]**: chosen by you, and only you should know it. It **proves** you are who you say you are.

blocks.text: Everyone needs a **unique login** so the network knows exactly who is using it. That way your files are kept private, nobody else can see or change your work, and anything done on an account can be traced back to the right person.
Setting a strong password

head: A strong password should…
A strong password should NOT…
rows: Be just a name (yours, your dog's or your team's)
Use some numbers and symbols like $, %, !
Be the same as your username
Be the same as any other password you have used

blocks.title: Worked example: making a password stronger
blocks.context: Jack supports Ballinamallard United and wants to use the password *ballinamallard*.
steps: It is just a name, and people who know Jack could guess it: **weak**.
Make it longer and mix the case: *Ballina-Mallard*.
Add numbers and symbols: *Ballina!Mallard_74*.
Better still, use three random words joined together: *Kettle7!Otter$Rain*.
blocks.answer: Kettle7!Otter$Rain is strong: over 8 characters, capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols, and not linked to Jack.

blocks.text: Never write the example passwords on this page down and use them. They are now public! Make up your own, and you may be asked to change it during the year.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The server controls the network, stores files centrally and shares printers; you use a workstation.
The school network is part of C2k, used across Northern Ireland.
Your User ID is unique; your password proves who you are and must stay secret.
Strong password: 8+ characters, capitals and lower case, numbers, symbols; not a name, not your username, not reused.

pages.spec: Explain the difference between files and folders, recognise common file extensions and organise work in a folder structure
pages.summary: Files hold your work; folders hold files. Using a sensible folder structure with meaningful names means you can always find your work quickly, keep backups easily and avoid saving the same file in several places.

blocks.text: Files and folders

A **[[file]]** is one piece of saved work, such as an essay, a photo or a song. A **[[folder]]** is a container that holds files (and other folders) so they are grouped and organised, just like the ring binders in your schoolbag hold your worksheets.

blocks.text: File extensions

The **[[file extension]]** is the part after the dot at the end of a file name. It tells the computer what type of file it is and which program should open it. Microsoft Word documents end in **.docx**, Excel spreadsheets in **.xlsx** and PowerPoint presentations in **.pptx**.

blocks.text: Sorceress Alice's folder structure

Alice has a **[[root folder]]** called *Year 8*. Inside it are five subject folders: Science, Maths, ICT, English and History. Inside those are topic folders: **Science → Space**; **ICT → Spreadsheets, Databases**; **English → Poems, Haiku, Macbeth**. (Maths and History have no topic folders yet.)

steps: **Marks.xlsx** is an Excel spreadsheet, so it belongs in ICT's Spreadsheets folder: *Year 8 > ICT > Spreadsheets*.

blocks.text: Why organise your files?

items: It is much **easier to find** files: you always know where to look and never waste time wondering where to save something.
You can easily **direct someone**, such as your teacher, to a file.
It is easier to keep **[[backup|backups]]**.
You don't save files in several places, or save the same file again because you can't find the first copy.
It is **more efficient**: less storage is wasted on duplicate copies, and you find files quickly when time is short.

blocks.text: In school, save work in your own area on the network, inside a sensible path such as *Year 8 > ICT > Unit 1*. If the folders aren't there, create them, and always give files **meaningful names** like *Email Quiz.docx*, not *Document1.docx*.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A file is one item of work; a folder is a container for files and folders.
File extensions (.docx, .jpg, .mp3…) show the type of file.
Organise files in a structure: root folder > subject > topic.
Organised files are quicker to find, easier to back up and don't waste storage.

pages.spec: Explain what email is, what you need to use it, and the rules of netiquette
pages.summary: Email is electronic mail sent between computers over the internet. You need an account, email software and internet access. Good netiquette means being polite, always using a subject line, avoiding capitals and text language.

blocks.text: **[[Email]]** stands for **electronic mail**. It is a message sent from one computer to another over the internet.
What you need to use email

head: You need…
Examples
rows: Gmail, Yahoo, AOL, Hotmail/Outlook.com, or your school C2k account
Outlook, webmail in a browser, Thunderbird
From an internet provider such as BT, Virgin Media, TalkTalk or Plusnet
blocks.caption: The three things you need to send email

blocks.text: Netiquette

Just like sending a letter, sending an email follows rules. Email is a fairly **formal** way to message someone, so it should be professional. **[[Netiquette]]** (net + etiquette) is how you should behave when sending emails and using the internet:

items: **Be polite.**
**Never forget the subject line**: whoever receives your email needs to know what it is about.
**Do not type in ALL CAPITALS**: it looks like you are SHOUTING.
**Don't use text language** (like *c u l8r*), not even when emailing friends.
Show you are joking with a smiley :) . [[Emoticon|Emoticons]] are fine in informal emails to friends, but not in formal emails to a teacher or a boss.

blocks.text: Sender and recipient

The **[[sender]]** is the person who sends the email. The **[[recipient]]** is the person who receives it. When a message is sent, a copy is kept in the sender's **Sent** folder and the message appears in the recipient's **[[inbox]]**. The recipient opens it to read it.
Your school email address

Your school email address is the **username you use to log in to the school computers**, followed by **@c2ken.net**. For example, if your username is *aperson123*, your email address is **aperson123@c2ken.net**.
Write your school email address in your planner so you always have it.
Reading your school email

The school uses **Microsoft Outlook**. In your inbox, new (unread) emails have a **blue bar**, the **sender** is shown in **bold**, the **subject** is in blue and a **preview** of the start of the message appears underneath. You can also see when it was sent. Double-click an email to open and read it in full.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Email = electronic mail, sent between computers over the internet.
You need an email account, email software and internet access.
Netiquette: be polite, always add a subject, no ALL CAPS, no text language.
Sender sends; recipient receives the email in their inbox.
School email = your login username + @c2ken.net.

pages.spec: Send an email from school, and use CC, BCC, reply, forward and attachments correctly
pages.summary: You send school email through MySchool > Office 365 > Outlook. CC sends a visible copy, BCC a hidden copy. Replying (RE:) goes back to the sender, forwarding (FW:) passes the email on, and a paperclip shows an attachment.

blocks.text: Sending an email in school

items: Open the internet and log in to **MySchool**.
Click on **Office 365**.
Select **Outlook**.
Select **New Message**.
Type the email address of the recipient, e.g. a friend in your class.
Add a **meaningful subject line**.
Type your message using suitable language, e.g. tell them a little about yourself: your favourite team, a film or music artist you like, a game you recently played.
**Sign off** with your name so they know who it is from.
Click **Send**.

blocks.text: CC and BCC
Under the **To** box you will see **CC**, and sometimes **BCC**. These are useful when emailing more than one person.

head: CC (carbon copy)
BCC (blind carbon copy)
rows: Copying your form teacher into an email to Mr Butler
A club newsletter sent to 1000 people, so nobody's address is shown to the others

blocks.text: BCC is a bit like a company sending a newsletter: you get your copy, but you can't see the 999 other people who were sent it, and they can't see your address.
Replying and forwarding

**[[Reply|Replying]]** sends a message **back** to the person who sent the email to you. The address is filled in automatically and **RE:** appears in front of the subject. **[[Forward|Forwarding]]** sends the email **on** to someone else. **FW:** (or **Fwd:**) appears in front of the subject.

blocks.title: Worked example: Alex, Jack and Robert
blocks.context: Alex sends an email with the subject *Rugby training* to Jack.
steps: Jack receives it in his inbox. Alex is the sender; Jack is the recipient.
Jack **replies** to Alex: the email goes back to Alex with the subject *RE: Rugby training*.
Jack **forwards** it to Robert: Robert gets Alex's message with the subject *FW: Rugby training*.
blocks.answer: Reply = back to the sender (RE:). Forward = on to someone new (FW:).

blocks.text: Attachments

An **[[attachment]]** is a file sent with an email, such as a Word document or a photo. When an email has an attachment, a **paperclip icon** appears next to it. You can open the email and then open or save the attachment. To add one, click **Attach** (the paperclip) in a new message and choose the file.

blocks.title: Worked example: the Sending Email practical quiz
blocks.context: You save a Word document called *Quick Quiz* in *Year 8 > ICT > Email*, answer six questions in it and email it to your teacher as an attachment.
steps: Q1 What does email stand for? **Electronic mail.**
Q2 Difference between replying and forwarding? **Replying sends the email back to the person who sent it; forwarding sends it on to someone else.**

Q3 Difference between the internet and the WWW? **The internet is the physical network of connected computers (hardware); the WWW is the collection of websites on it (the software you reach with a browser).**
Q4 What does netiquette mean? **How you should behave when sending emails and using the internet.**
Q5 Three tasks search engines perform? **Crawling, indexing and retrieval.**
Q6 How to add an attachment? **Click the paperclip/Attach button and choose the file.**
For full marks the email itself also needs a professional subject line, a suitable attachment name, a greeting, a clear message and your name to sign off.
blocks.answer: A good email: subject + greeting + message + sign-off + correctly named attachment.

items: Send school email: MySchool > Office 365 > Outlook > New Message.
CC = visible copy; BCC = hidden copy.
Reply goes back to the sender (RE:); forward goes to someone new (FW:).
A paperclip icon means the email has an attachment.

pages.spec: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web, and how search engines work
pages.summary: The internet is the physical network of connected computers (hardware); the World Wide Web is the websites stored on it (software), viewed in a browser. Search engines use algorithms to crawl, index and retrieve web pages.

blocks.text: The internet and the WWW are not the same thing

head: The internet
The World Wide Web (WWW)
rows: A massive global network of computers linked together
The collection of millions of websites stored on the internet
Email, online gaming, video calls, the web and more
Through a connection such as WiFi or broadband

blocks.text: The **[[internet]]** is the **hardware**: millions of computers linked by cables (including under the sea!), routers and satellites. The **[[World Wide Web]]** is just **one service** that runs on the internet. You view it with a **[[web browser]]** such as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox or Safari.
Think of the internet as the **roads** and the WWW as the **shops** you visit using those roads. Email and online gaming also use the roads, but they are not shops on the web.
Search engines
A **[[search engine]]**, such as Google or Bing, helps you find pages on the WWW. Search engines use complex **[[algorithm|algorithms]]** (sets of step-by-step rules) to do three tasks:

head: Task
What happens
rows: Programs called web crawlers (or spiders) follow links to discover websites.
Each website is analysed and stored in a huge database called an index.
When you search, you receive a list of relevant web pages, with the most relevant at the top.
blocks.caption: The three tasks of a search engine

blocks.text: The web is enormous. In 2020 the indexed web held at least **6.51 billion** pages, and back in 2013 Google said its index already held information about 30 trillion pages and used 100 million gigabytes of storage. It has grown hugely since.
The top result is not always true! Anyone can publish on the web, so check information on more than one trustworthy site.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Internet = global network of connected computers (hardware).
WWW = the websites on the internet (software), viewed in a web browser.
Search engines crawl, index and retrieve web pages using algorithms.
The most relevant results appear at the top, but always check they are reliable.

pages.spec: Describe what a computer virus can do and how to avoid one
pages.summary: A virus is a harmful program designed to damage a computer or make it unreliable: corrupting and deleting files, stealing personal information or slowing it down. Avoid them by not opening unknown attachments, using up-to-date anti-virus software and only downloading safely.

blocks.text: A computer **[[virus]]** is a program designed to **deliberately damage** a computer system or make it **unreliable**. Like a cold virus, it spreads from one computer to another, often hidden inside an email attachment, a download or a USB stick.
What can a virus do?

items: **Corrupt** (scramble) files and folders so they won't open.
**Delete** data.
**Steal** your personal information, such as passwords.
Infect your computer so it **slows down** or **stops working**.

blocks.text: How to avoid viruses

head: Do this…
Because…
rows: Don't open email attachments from people you don't know
Attachments are one of the most common ways viruses spread.
Install anti-virus software and keep it up to date
New viruses appear every day; old anti-virus software won't recognise them.
Only download files from known, safe sites, with permission from a parent or guardian
Free games, mods and films from unknown sites often hide viruses.
Scan USB memory sticks before opening files on them
A stick that has been in an infected computer can carry the virus to yours.
blocks.caption: Ways to stay virus-free

blocks.text: **[[Anti-virus software]]** scans files, emails and USB sticks, looking for known viruses, and removes or quarantines (locks away) anything it finds. This is one reason why you must never try to install software or plug in unknown devices on the school network.

blocks.title: Worked example: should Ciara open it?
blocks.context: Ciara gets an email from an address she doesn't recognise. The subject is *You've won a free PS5!!!* and it has an attachment called *claim_prize.exe*.
steps: She doesn't know the sender, so this is a warning sign.
The offer is too good to be true, which is another warning sign.
The attachment is a program (.exe), which could install a virus if opened.
blocks.answer: No. Ciara should not open the attachment, should not reply, and should tell an adult or delete the email.

blocks.text: Never try to bring a virus onto the school network, even "as a joke". It breaks the Acceptable Use Policy and can be against the law.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A virus is a program designed to damage a computer or make it unreliable.
Viruses can corrupt or delete files, steal personal information and slow a computer down.
Don't open attachments from strangers.
Use up-to-date anti-virus software, download only from safe sites with permission, and scan USB sticks.

pages.spec: Know the three things we keep safe when using computers and what a hazard is
pages.summary: When using ICT we must keep the equipment, our data and ourselves safe. A hazard is anything that could cause damage, harm or ill health. Most safety rules are common sense, and anything dangerous should be reported.

blocks.text: When you use computers, there are **three** things you need to keep safe:

items: **The equipment**: the computers, screens, keyboards and cables.
**Our data**: our files, work and personal information.
**Ourselves**: our bodies and our health.

blocks.text: We follow **[[health and safety]]** rules to keep ourselves from harm. Most of the rules are **common sense**: we just need to behave sensibly. If something looks dangerous, **report it** to the person in charge (in the ICT room, that's your teacher).
Your data is your own, too. Be careful about where you share it and who you share your personal information with.
What is a hazard?

A **[[hazard]]** is a danger or risk: any source of potential **damage, harm or adverse (bad) health effects** on something or someone. Failing to stick to health and safety rules can result in injury.
Hazards in the ICT classroom

head: Hazard
What could happen
How to combat it
rows: Someone trips and falls, or pulls equipment off a desk
Tidy cables away under desks or in cable covers
Spills cause electric shocks or damage keyboards
No food or drink in the ICT room
Bags and coats on the floor
Put bags under desks, keep walkways clear
Don't plug too many devices into one socket; use proper extension leads
Don't touch it; report it to the teacher straight away
Room too hot, poor air flow
Open windows, use air conditioning or fans, keep vents clear
blocks.caption: Example hazards and solutions (the homework asks for five)

blocks.text: When you spot a hazard, think **Spot it, Stop it, Report it**.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Keep three things safe: the equipment, our data and ourselves.
A hazard is any source of potential damage, harm or bad health effects.
Most safety rules are common sense.
If something looks dangerous, report it to the person in charge.

diagram.title: Spot it, Stop it, Report it
diagram.caption: What to do when you see a hazard.

items.detail: Notice anything dangerous, like a loose cable or a spilled drink.

items.label: Stop it
items.detail: Stop using the equipment and warn people nearby. Don't try to fix electrics yourself.

items.label: Report it
items.detail: Tell the person in charge (your teacher) straight away.

items.label: Check it
items.detail: Once it's fixed, keep following the rules so it doesn't happen again.

pages.spec: Explain what causes backache when using computers and how to prevent it
pages.summary: Sitting in the same position for a long time, or on a chair at the wrong height, can cause backache and even damage the spine. Use an adjustable chair and a footrest, take regular breaks and don't slouch.

blocks.text: Back against the wall

**[[Backache]]** can be caused by sitting for long periods of time in the **same position**, or by having your **chair at the wrong height**. If this isn't dealt with, it could even cause **damage to the spine**.

Think about a long gaming session at home: hunched forward on the edge of the bed, staring at the TV for three hours. Your back is curved the whole time, and the next day it aches. The same thing can happen at a school or office desk.
How to combat backache

head: Solution
How it helps
rows: You can set the height and back support to fit your body.
Getting up and moving stops your muscles getting stiff.
If your feet don't reach the floor, a footrest supports your legs and back.
Good [[posture]] keeps your spine in its natural shape.
blocks.caption: Ways to combat backache

blocks.text: Good sitting posture

items: Sit back in the chair so your lower back is supported.
Keep your feet flat on the floor (or on a footrest).
Knees roughly level with your hips.
Shoulders relaxed, not hunched.
Screen at about eye level, straight in front of you.

blocks.text: Every 20–30 minutes, stand up, stretch and move about for a minute.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Backache is caused by sitting too long in one position or on a chair at the wrong height.
Left untreated, it can damage the spine.
Combat it with an adjustable chair, regular breaks, a footrest and good posture (no slouching).

pages.spec: Explain what causes eye strain and how to prevent it
pages.summary: Eye strain is caused by looking at a screen for a long time, and glare from bright lights makes it worse. It can cause headaches, sore eyes and worse eyesight. Combat it with breaks, blinds, sensible screen positions and anti-glare screens.

blocks.text: A sight for sore eyes

**[[Eye strain]]** is caused by continuously looking at a screen for a long period of time. **Reflection** and **[[glare]]** from bright lights, such as sunlight shining on the screen, can make it worse.
Constantly straining your eyes can result in:

items: **Headaches**
**Sore eyes**
A **worsening of your eyesight**

blocks.text: How to combat eye strain

head: Solution
How it helps
rows: Text and images are big enough to read without squinting.
Gives your eyes a rest from focusing on the screen.
Stops bright sunlight causing glare on the screen.
Position your monitor away from direct sunlight
An [[anti-glare screen]] has a coating that cuts down reflections.
blocks.caption: Ways to combat eye strain

blocks.text: Try the **20-20-20 rule**: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. Looking out the window towards the hills works well!
Phones count too. Scrolling for hours in bed in a dark room is a classic recipe for tired, sore eyes.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Eye strain comes from looking at a screen for too long; glare and reflections make it worse.
It can cause headaches, sore eyes and worse eyesight.
Combat it with a suitable screen size, regular breaks, blinds, keeping the monitor out of direct sunlight and anti-glare screens.

pages.spec: Explain what Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) is and how to prevent it
pages.summary: RSI happens when you make the same movement again and again, usually affecting the wrists and fingers. It can cause extreme pain and joint damage. Prevent it with an angled keyboard, a wrist rest, straight wrists and regular breaks.

blocks.text: Day after day after day
**[[Repetitive Strain Injury]]** (**RSI**) happens when you constantly make the **same movement** again and again. It usually affects the **joints in your wrists and fingers**.

Ever played a game for a long time and got sore or numb thumbs? This has been called **"Nintendo thumb"**. Typing, texting, clicking a mouse and pressing controller buttons are all repeated movements that can lead to RSI.
RSI can cause **extreme pain** and **damage to the joints**. In extreme cases it can lead to arthritis (painful, swollen joints).
How to combat RSI

head: Solution
How it helps
rows: Adjust your keyboard to a comfortable angle
Your hands and wrists aren't bent awkwardly.
A [[wrist rest]] supports your wrists so they stay straight.
Keep your wrists straight when typing
Bent wrists put extra strain on the joints.
Gives the muscles and joints a rest from repeating the same movement.
blocks.caption: Ways to combat RSI

blocks.title: Worked example: Conor's gaming marathon
blocks.context: Conor plays a football game on his console for four hours without stopping. His thumbs and wrists are sore and tingly the next day.
steps: The cause: repeating the same thumb movements for hours = a risk of RSI (Nintendo thumb).
Fix 1: take a break every 30–45 minutes and stretch his hands.
Fix 2: hold the controller in a relaxed way, keeping his wrists straight.
Fix 3: limit very long sessions.
blocks.answer: Conor is showing early signs of RSI; regular breaks and good hand position will help.

blocks.title: Key points
items: RSI = Repetitive Strain Injury, caused by making the same movement again and again.
It usually affects joints in the wrists, fingers and thumbs ('Nintendo thumb').
It can cause extreme pain, joint damage and even arthritis.
Combat it with an angled keyboard, a wrist rest, straight wrists and regular breaks.

pages.spec: Explain what ergonomics is and give examples of ergonomic design
pages.summary: Ergonomics is the science of designing safe, comfortable hardware and furniture for humans. Companies spend a lot on ergonomic controllers and chairs so people can use them longer, but you still need to look after your own health.

blocks.text: **[[Ergonomics]]** is the science concerned with designing **safe and comfortable hardware and office furniture for humans**. In other words, it is designing equipment that fits the human body.
Ergonomics in games consoles

items: PlayStation officially changed the design of its PS4 controller **three** times, and there are hundreds more controllers on the market.
Microsoft spent **"hundreds of millions"** designing its Xbox One controller.

blocks.text: Why spend so much? A comfortable controller means you can play for longer with less chance of getting sore or needing a break. That's good for the companies, because you keep using their products. **It's very important to remember to keep your own safety in mind** however comfortable the equipment feels.
Examples of ergonomic equipment

Ergonomic feature
Problem it helps

pages.spec: Describe threats to data and how to keep data safe
pages.summary: As well as protecting ourselves, we must protect our data. Threats include hackers, viruses, system crashes, accidental deletion and insider threats from employees. Backups, passwords, anti-virus software and good file management keep data safe.

blocks.text: As well as keeping ourselves protected when using ICT, we need to protect our **data** from being damaged. This is called **[[cyber security]]**. One big threat is the **[[hacker]]**: an unauthorised person who breaks into a system.
Threats to data

head: Threat
What happens
rows: Unauthorised users (hackers) gain access to data by illegal means.
Hackers often use viruses, which can attack and seriously damage files.
A crash affecting the hard drive may damage key sections of data.
Data can be lost accidentally or deleted by mistake.
Data can be sabotaged by former employees committing malicious (deliberately harmful) acts.
blocks.caption: Threats to our data

blocks.text: Insider threats

An **[[insider threat]]** comes from someone *inside* an organisation. It isn't always on purpose. Some employees cause damage by being **careless**, for example clicking a dodgy link or leaving a laptop on a bus. These careless insiders are sometimes called **pawns** or **goofs**, depending on the situation. You'll learn more about these at GCSE.
Keeping data safe: every problem has a solution

head: Problem
Solution
rows: Organise work in sensible folders with meaningful file names; use the computer's search tool to look for them.
Keep regular backups on another device or in the cloud (e.g. your school network area or Google Drive) so the work can be restored.
Use up-to-date anti-virus software to scan and remove it; restore a clean copy from a backup.
Search by date modified or by a word in the file; sort the folder by date; next time use meaningful names.
Password goes missing or is forgotten
Use the 'forgotten password' reset (or ask the network technician/teacher in school), then set a new strong password and never write it where others can see it.
blocks.caption: Keeping Data Safe: answers

blocks.text: The best protection against nearly every data problem is a **backup**: a second copy, kept somewhere else.

blocks.title: Key points
items: We must protect our data as well as ourselves.
Threats: hackers, viruses, system crashes, accidental loss and insider threats.
Insider threats can be deliberate or careless.
Backups, strong passwords, anti-virus software and organised folders keep data safe.

pages.spec: Know the law on health and safety at work and eight things employers must do to keep ICT users safe
pages.summary: Employers have a duty of care to employees. The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 and the Display Screen Equipment Regulations mean employers must provide things such as adjustable chairs, tiltable screens, anti-glare filters, breaks and eye tests.

blocks.text: Employers have a **[[duty of care]]** to their **[[employee|employees]]** when they use ICT. This means they are legally responsible for keeping them safe.
The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

This is covered by the **[[Health and Safety at Work Act]]**, introduced in **1974**. It keeps employees, employers, data and equipment safe when people use ICT, or any computer-related equipment, as part of their job. It sets out the general duties that:

items: **employers** have towards employees and members of the public;
**employees** have to themselves and to each other;
certain **self-employed** people have towards themselves and others.

blocks.text: The Act provides the legal framework to promote, stimulate and encourage high standards of health and safety in workplaces. It protects employees and the public from work activities, including those that involve IT.

In Northern Ireland, the same duties come from the **Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978**, which matches the 1974 Act. The detailed rules for computer users are the **Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992**, which apply across the UK including NI.
Eight employer regulations for ICT users

head: Employers must…
This protects against…
rows: Eye strain, neck and back ache
Provide **foot supports** (footrests) for those who need them
Plan the work so employees get **regular breaks** or changes of activity

pages.spec: Explain what an algorithm is and put instructions into a correct sequence
pages.summary: An algorithm is a sequence of clear, short, specific instructions to complete a task or solve a problem, like a recipe or directions. Algorithms are translated into code in a programming language so a computer can follow them.

blocks.text: An **[[algorithm]]** is a sequence of instructions, or a set of rules, that are followed to complete a task or solve a problem. The task can be anything, as long as you can give **clear, short and specific** instructions for it.
Everyday algorithms

items: A **recipe** for baking a cake.
**Directions** to a place: "Turn right after the bank, walk straight to the traffic lights, turn right…"
The steps for starting a lesson: come in and sit down quietly, log on, open a browser, search for a word, then turn off your monitor when you've finished.

blocks.text: Computers and algorithms

Computers are very good at carrying out a **[[sequence]]** of precisely defined instructions. An algorithm could be simple (work out 25 ÷ 5, or check if a number is prime) or complex (study the pages you like on social media and decide which adverts to show you).

Computers don't actually understand algorithms written in English. An algorithm must be translated into **[[code]]**, written in a **[[programming language]]** such as **Scratch**, **Python** or **C#**. Different languages suit different jobs, and game developers sometimes use several languages in the same game!

blocks.title: Worked example: the zebra crossing
blocks.context: A zebra crossing on a wide road has an island in the middle. Put the instructions in order (traffic in the UK drives on the left, so the first half of the road has traffic coming from your right).
steps: 1. Stop at the side of the road looking to the other side of the zebra crossing
2. Look right
3. Wait until traffic from the right has stopped or the road is clear
4. Step onto the first half of the zebra crossing
5. Walk to the island looking both ways and listening
6. Stop at the island
7. Look left
8. Stay on the island until traffic from the left has stopped or the road is clear
9. Step onto the second half of the zebra crossing
10. Walk to the other side of the road looking both ways and listening
blocks.answer: Putting the instructions in the correct order creates a sequence.

blocks.title: Worked example: making a cuppa
blocks.context: Place the flowchart instructions in order to make a cup of tea.
steps: Start → Boil water → Put teabag in teapot → Add water → Remove teabag from teapot → Pour tea into cup → Pour milk into cup → Add sugar → Drink tea → Stop
blocks.answer: Is there only one correct sequence? No: you could add sugar before milk, for example. But some steps must come first (you can't pour the tea before adding the water).

blocks.title: Worked example: the second river crossing
blocks.context: A man and a woman weigh 100 kg each and two children weigh 50 kg each. Their boat can carry up to 100 kg. How can all four cross the river?
steps: 1. Both children cross (100 kg).
2. One child rows back.
3. The man crosses alone (100 kg).
4. The other child rows back.
5. Both children cross again.
6. One child rows back.
7. The woman crosses alone.
8. The other child rows back.
9. Both children cross. Everyone is over!
blocks.answer: 9 crossings. The children do the shuttling, because only they can travel together.

Recipes and directions are everyday algorithms.
The order (sequence) of the instructions matters.

pages.spec: Compare computer control with human control and give advantages and disadvantages
pages.summary: Computers don't need breaks or pay, repeat actions identically and can work in danger, but they only know what they are programmed to do, need power and can be expensive. Traffic lights versus a police officer directing traffic is a good example.

blocks.text: Which is better at controlling traffic: **automatic traffic lights** or a **police officer** standing in the junction? Using a computer to run a system like this is called **[[computer control]]**. Both have good and bad points.
Advantages of computer control

items: Computers do **not need breaks**.
They do **not take sick days or holidays**.
They can **repeat actions in an identical way** indefinitely (forever).
They can **work in environments that are dangerous** for people.
They **don't need to be paid**.
They can process data from **[[sensor|sensors]]** very quickly.
They can manage **hundreds or thousands of inputs** at the same time.
They can make **reliable and accurate** decisions.

blocks.text: Disadvantages of computer control

items: Computers are **only as good as their programming**, which may contain errors.
When faced with conditions **not covered in their programming**, they won't know what to do.
**Underpowered** computers might take too long in a time-critical (urgent) situation.
They **rely on power**: in a power cut the program won't work.
They may **cost a lot** to buy, maintain and develop.

head: Traffic lights (computer)
Police officer (human)

Expensive to install, but no wages

blocks.title: Worked example: who should run the junction?
blocks.context: A busy junction in Enniskillen town centre needs controlling every day of the year.
steps: Normal traffic every day: traffic lights are better: cheap to run, never tired, consistent.
A crash or a power cut: a police officer is better, because they can adapt to something the lights weren't programmed for.
blocks.answer: Use computer control for the everyday job, with humans ready for the unexpected.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Computer control: no breaks, no pay, identical repetition, works in danger, fast and accurate.
But: only as good as its programming, can't handle unplanned situations, needs power, can be expensive.
Humans can adapt and think; computers can't.

pages.spec: Know that computers use binary, and explain what a variable is and why programs use them
pages.summary: Computers understand only 0s and 1s, called binary. Programmers use variables: named boxes in memory that store values like numbers, text or true/false, and can change while the program runs, making programs reusable.

blocks.text: Binary: the computer's language

Computers and games consoles understand a very simple language: just **0s and 1s**. That's a lot fewer than the 26 letters in our alphabet! This language is called **[[binary]]**. Computers read millions (even billions) of these 1s and 0s every second.
Each 0 or 1 is like a tiny switch that is either **off (0)** or **on (1)**. Everything on your phone, from photos to songs to messages, is stored as huge patterns of 0s and 1s.
What is a variable?

Humans program computers, often using **[[variable|variables]]**. A variable is a **location in memory** where you can **temporarily store text or numbers**. It is like an empty box with a label on it, or the memory button on a calculator. You choose a name for the box (the *variable name*) and your **[[program]]** can change what's inside.

blocks.title: Worked example: changing a variable
blocks.context: What is stored in X at the end?
steps: `X = 50` puts 50 in the box called X.
`X = X + 5` takes what's in X (50), adds 5, and puts the answer back in X.
blocks.answer: X now holds 55.

blocks.text: Variables describe things

Think of a character in a game like The Sims. What makes one character different from another? Each difference is a variable: **hair style** (long/short/combed/frizzy), **hair colour** (black/blue/blonde), **glasses** (yes/no), **top** (tank/T-shirt/shirt), **shorts**, **footwear** (trainers/boots/shoes), **piercings**, **tattoos**, and of course **name**, **age** and **interests**. There are literally thousands of possible variables!
Why variables make programs better

blocks.title: Worked example: a calculator program
blocks.context: Compare a program with no variables to one that uses variables.
steps: **Version 1:** START → SET answer AS 2 × 4 → PRINT answer → END. It always prints 8. Not very useful!
**Version 2:** START → INPUT number1 → INPUT number2 → SET answer AS number1 × number2 → PRINT answer → END.
Run Version 2 with 6 and 7: answer = 6 × 7 = **42**. Run it again with 12 and 3: answer = **36**.
blocks.answer: Version 2 is slightly longer, but it works for any two numbers, so it is far more usable.

blocks.text: Variables make programs **reusable**: for example, displaying your name at the top of the screen or keeping a score in a game. They can store **text**, **numbers** and even **true/false** values, and let the program store, change and use these values while it runs.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Computers understand binary: just 0s and 1s.
A variable is a named location in memory that temporarily stores a value.
X = X + 5 adds 5 to whatever is stored in X.
Variables can hold numbers, text and true/false values, and make programs reusable.

blocks.text: The **[[BBC micro:bit]]** is a **pocket-sized, codable computer** with 25 red [[LED|LEDs]] on the front. You can use it to flash messages, create games, invent digital stories, act as a games controller or even pause and skip songs on a playlist.

head: Part
What it does
rows: A 5 × 5 grid of lights that can show text, numbers and pictures
Two programmable buttons used as inputs
Motion detector: senses shaking and tilting
Detects which direction it is facing
Connects to other micro:bits or devices wirelessly
Plug into a computer to load programs and power it

blocks.text: Finding an LED: coordinates

The LEDs are in a **5 × 5 grid**. Like coordinates in Maths, each LED has an **x** (across) and a **y** (down) value. Unlike Maths, the numbers **start at 0** in the **top-left corner** and go up to 4, and **y counts downwards**.

blocks.title: Worked example: which LED is (3, 1)?
blocks.context: Find the LED at (3, 1).
steps: x = 3: count across from the left: 0, 1, 2, **3**. That's the 4th column.
y = 1: count down from the top: 0, **1**. That's the 2nd row.
blocks.answer: (3, 1) is the LED in the 4th column, 2nd row.

blocks.text: Data types

Every value in a program has a **[[data type]]**, which tells the computer what kind of data it is, such as an [[integer]] (whole number). For example, the micro:bit's `show string` block displays text, and `show number` displays a number.

pages.spec: Explain selection (IF/ELSE) and the two types of loop
pages.summary: Selection uses an IF statement: code runs only if a condition is true, and ELSE gives something else to do if it is false. Loops repeat code: count-controlled loops repeat a set number of times; condition-controlled loops repeat while a condition is true.

blocks.text: Selection: IF and ELSE

When programming, we use a **[[condition]]** (a test that is true or false) to decide if a piece of code should run. This is called **[[selection]]**, and it uses an **IF statement**. A piece of code inside the IF will **only run if the condition is true**.
IF statements are usually paired with **ELSE**. If the condition is **not** true, the code in the ELSE part runs instead.

blocks.title: Worked example: IF … ELSE on a micro:bit
blocks.context: `if myValue = 10 then` show a tick `else` show a cross. What appears?
steps: If myValue is 10: the condition is **true**, so a tick is shown.
If myValue is 7: the condition is **false**, so the ELSE part runs and a cross is shown.
blocks.answer: Only one of the two branches ever runs.

blocks.text: Loops
A **[[loop]]** means **to repeat**. Loops (also called **iteration**) let code be repeated without retyping it over and over. We could loop 2 or 3 times, 5, 100, or even forever. There are two types:

head: Count-controlled loop
Condition-controlled loop
rows: As long as a condition is true
Do we know how many times?
No, it depends on when the condition changes

blocks.text: In a **[[condition-controlled loop]]**, the condition is checked **before each repeat**. If it is true, the code inside runs; then the condition is checked again. As soon as it is false, the loop stops. A **[[count-controlled loop]]** is used when you know exactly how many repeats you need.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracing a while loop
blocks.context: myValue starts at 7. The loop is `while myValue < 10: add 1 to myValue`.
steps: 7 < 10 is true → myValue becomes 8.
8 < 10 is true → myValue becomes 9.
9 < 10 is true → myValue becomes 10.
10 < 10 is false → the loop stops.
blocks.answer: The loop ran 3 times and myValue ends at 10.

blocks.text: Ask yourself: *do I know how many times?* Yes → count-controlled (repeat/for). No → condition-controlled (while).

blocks.title: Key points
items: Selection uses IF: code runs only if a condition is true.
ELSE runs when the condition is false.
Loop = repeat (iteration).
Count-controlled (for) loops repeat a set number of times.
Condition-controlled (while) loops repeat while a condition is true.

diagram.title: A condition-controlled loop
diagram.caption: The condition is checked before every repeat.

nodes.label: Start
nodes.detail: Set myValue to 7.

nodes.label: myValue < 10?
nodes.detail: A decision: true → run the loop body; false → leave the loop.

nodes.label: Add 1 to myValue
nodes.detail: The loop body, then go back and check the condition again.

nodes.label: End
nodes.detail: Reached once myValue is 10.

check.why: A loop repeats code.

check.q: `repeat 4 times` is an example of which loop?
check.why: We know it will repeat exactly 4 times.

check.why: ELSE runs when the condition is false.

practice.a: A count-controlled loop repeats a set/known number of times (1); a condition-controlled loop repeats while a condition is true, so the number of repeats isn't known in advance (1).

pages.spec: Explain what e-safety is and why your privacy matters
pages.summary: E-safety is the safe and responsible use of technology: the internet, texts, gaming, email and smart devices. It is as much about how you behave as about security. Moving to secondary school, you become a more independent internet user, so knowing how to stay safe matters.

blocks.text: **[[E-safety]]** (or online safety) is the **safe, responsible and ethical** use of technology. This includes the internet, and other ways of communicating using electronic media: text messages, messaging apps, online gaming, email and smart connected devices.
E-safety isn't just the "common sense" stuff. In practice, e-safety is **as much about behaviour as it is about electronic security**: how you treat others, what you share and who you trust.
Why is your privacy important?

Have you ever had something private or secret about you get out? Online, it can spread much faster and much further. **[[Privacy]]** means keeping control of your personal information and who can see it.

head: Fact
What it tells us
rows: Nearly **1 in 3** 11–13 year olds have broadcast themselves live on the internet
Live streaming is common, and once it's out it can be recorded by anyone watching.
**81%** of 8–17 year olds say they know when and how to ask permission to post something about someone else
Most young people know they should ask first…
**52%** say someone they know shared a photo or video of them without asking
…but over half have had their own photo shared without permission.
**47%** of young people think it's important to 'fit in' online
Pressure to fit in can push people to share more than they should.
blocks.caption: Young people online: the facts

blocks.text: Becoming a good online citizen

As you move to secondary school you become a more independent and confident internet user with more varied habits. The internet can be hugely positive, but there are dangers if we use it wrongly. That's why we keep talking about online safety: so you become a good **[[online citizen]]**.

blocks.title: Worked example: why ask before posting a photo of a friend?
blocks.context: 52% of 8–17 year olds say someone shared a photo or video of them without asking. Why is asking for consent before posting photos of others an important part of good online behaviour?
steps: It is their image: they have a right to decide who sees it.
They might be embarrassed or upset by it, which could even become cyberbullying.
It could reveal personal information, like their school uniform or location.
Once posted, it can be copied and shared and can't be taken back.
blocks.answer: Always ask first, because you can't undo a post, and it's respectful.

blocks.title: Key points
items: E-safety = the safe and responsible use of technology.
It covers the internet, texts, gaming, email and smart devices.
E-safety is as much about behaviour as electronic security.
Always ask before posting a photo or video of someone else.

pages.spec: Make safe choices about photos, friends, posts and privacy settings
pages.summary: Photos posted online are there for ever. Only accept friends you know in real life, don't announce holidays or post personal details, use an avatar, and set your profile to private so only real friends can see it.

blocks.text: Becky's story (a video shown in class) is about a girl who shared too much online. These statements test what you'd do. Here are the answers.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to post a photo of yourself in your school uniform on social networking sites."

Your uniform shows where you go to school.
**Never** send photos to people you don't know, and never post pictures you wouldn't want your parents, teacher or grandparent to see.
Don't use your own photo as a profile picture. Use a cool graphic, called an **[[avatar]]**, instead.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to accept friends online even if you don't know them in person."
steps: Friends get access to more information about you, your other friends and your personal details.
The average person has around 55 real-life friends but over 200 online 'friends'.
Don't just add 'friends of friends': you have no idea who they really are.
Adults with bad intentions can pretend to be young people and try to contact children.

blocks.title: True or false?
blocks.context: "It is OK to post when I go on holiday."
steps: You've just told everyone your house is empty.
It wouldn't be nice to come home and find you'd been burgled.
Post your holiday photos **after** you get home.

blocks.context: "It is OK to update my status with personal information such as my phone number."

blocks.text: Think before you post

A funny or embarrassing photo of someone might seem harmless. But what happens when someone uses a photo like that to make **you** feel uncomfortable? **Never** post photos you wouldn't want your granny or your teacher to see. Employers often look up people's social media, and silly photos, even from when you were young and even ones you didn't post yourself, could affect whether you get a job.

pages.spec: Describe the risks of online gaming and how to stay safe
pages.summary: Online gaming lets you play in real time with people worldwide. Risks include offensive chat, strangers, griefing and in-game purchases running up big bills. Stay safe by telling parents who you play with, reporting abuse, protecting personal details and controlling purchases.

blocks.text: **[[Online gaming]]** means you can play **in real time** with people across the world through an electronic device. **91%** of children are gamers. The average Fortnite player spends **6–10 hours a week** playing, and **68.8%** of Fortnite players have spent money on in-game purchases.
What you need to know

head: Risk
What it means
rows: Some games let you chat to anyone in the world, through headsets or text boxes, so you may come across offensive language and bullying.
Not everyone online is who they say they are. Gamers you meet online are strangers.
Games encourage you to buy extras like skins and currency. These have run up large bills without people realising.
Deliberately spoiling other players' games through harassment or cheating; sometimes used as a tactic to win. You could end up bullying or being bullied.
blocks.caption: Online gaming risks

blocks.text: Keeping safe while gaming

items: **Tell your parents** who you play with online and who you meet and talk to.
**Use appropriate language** in live chat, and learn how to **report** abusive chat and block anti-social players.
On a tablet or phone, use **airplane mode** to play offline games, so you can't make accidental purchases or connect with strangers.
**Don't share personal information.** Keep gaming friends in the game rather than adding them to your other social networks.
**Never agree to meet** someone you only know from a game.
Ask a parent to set up **purchase controls** (e.g. a password for buying) on your console.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Ryan do?
blocks.context: Ryan, 12, is playing an online shooter. Another player, 'Pro_Gamer99', says he's 13, gives Ryan free V-Bucks and asks for his Snapchat so they can 'squad up' more.
steps: Free gifts and quickly moving to a private app are warning signs.
Ryan should not give his Snapchat or any personal details: keep game friends in the game.
He should tell a parent about the player, and block/report if he feels uncomfortable.
blocks.answer: Say no, keep chat in the game, tell a trusted adult.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Online gaming = real-time play with people worldwide; 91% of children game.
Risks: offensive chat, strangers, griefing and in-game purchases.
Tell parents who you play with, report abuse and protect personal details.
Use airplane mode or purchase controls to avoid surprise bills.

pages.spec: Describe the risks of downloading content, including malware, phishing, pharming and copyright
pages.summary: Downloading music, films and games is useful, but files from illegal or unknown sites can carry viruses, trojans, worms and spyware. Phishing and pharming trick you into giving away details, and illegal downloading breaks copyright law.

blocks.text: The internet lets you download video, music, games and other files on demand, which is a great benefit. But downloading can also expose you to **viruses** and **[[spyware]]**, and illegal downloading breaks the law.
Things to keep in mind

items: **Check what you are downloading.** The film and music industries monitor the internet for people downloading illegally.
Downloading from **illegal sites** also risks downloading viruses or spyware at the same time.
Malware can also arrive through **emails, pop-ups, shared files, USB drives** and connected devices.

blocks.text: Threats when downloading

head: Threat
What it is and what it does
rows: Harmful code that attaches to genuine programs, copies itself and corrupts or deletes files.
Malware disguised as something you want, like a free game mod or film, that secretly opens a 'back door' so attackers can get in.
Malware that spreads itself from computer to computer across a network, slowing everything down.
Secretly watch what you do and record your key presses to steal passwords and bank details.
Fake emails or messages pretending to be a real organisation (a bank, a school, a game company) to trick you into giving away details.
Secretly redirects you from a real website to a fake copy, to capture your login details.
Illegally downloading or sharing music, films or software, which breaks UK copyright law.

blocks.text: Free versions of paid games and films are a favourite hiding place for trojans. If it looks too good to be true, it probably is.

pages.spec: Describe the benefits and risks of social networking and apps, and the settings that keep you safe
pages.summary: Social networks let you chat, meet people with similar interests and share photos, but most have a minimum age of 13. Risks include location sharing, tags, information spreading and strangers. Manage privacy settings, tag approvals and location services.

blocks.text: **[[Social networking]]** sites are a huge favourite. They let you **stay in touch** with friends, **meet new people** with similar interests and **share photos and videos**. Used well, they're a great place to show your creativity.
Age limits

The **lower age limit** for most social networks is **13**. This includes Facebook, Instagram, X (Twitter), Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube accounts, Tumblr and Ask.fm. Many include instant messaging for private conversations, and let you add friends, including people you don't know.
Three settings to manage
Check your [[privacy settings]], tag approvals and location services on every app you use.

head: Setting
Why it matters
rows: Set them to the strongest level so only close friends can search for you, see your posts or share them.
Approve or dismiss [[tag|tags]] before they appear on your profile, so you control what you're linked to.
Some apps use your phone's location. Turn it off so people can't see where you are.
blocks.caption: Critical settings

blocks.text: Risks of social networking

items: App versions of social networks can use your **phone's location**.
Information shared between friends can be **easily copied** and spread widely.
It isn't easy to **take back** a post, and it's impossible once it's been shared.
Not everyone you meet online is **who they say they are**. Chatrooms and forums connect complete strangers and may not be moderated (checked).
Chatrooms and forums are places **online groomers** go to contact children. Some include sexual language and online flirting, sometimes over video chat.

blocks.text: Safety issues with apps

head: Safety issue
Details
rows: Meeting and chatting with strangers online risks grooming and abuse, both online and offline.
Many apps share where you are. This can put children at risk from people who want to meet them in the real world, and raises worries about identity theft and privacy.
Behind a screen, some people feel bolder about pressuring others into sending offensive or inappropriate messages and images.
blocks.caption: App safety issues

blocks.text: Snapchat's Snap Map shows friends where you are unless you turn on **Ghost Mode**. Check this setting!

blocks.title: Key points
items: Social networks let you chat, meet people and share, but most have a minimum age of 13.
Manage privacy settings, tag approvals and location services.
Posts can be copied and spread and are hard to take back.
Strangers, location sharing and pressure to send content are key app risks.

check.why: Most set 13 as the lower age limit.

o: So people can't see where you are
check.why: Location sharing can let strangers find you.

o: Approve or dismiss tags before they appear on your profile
check.why: They give you control over what you're tagged in.

check.q: Why is it hard to take back a post?
o: Phones don't have a delete button
It may already have been copied and shared
check.why: Once shared, it's out of your control.

practice.a: Privacy settings: restrict who sees your posts (1); tag approvals: control what you're tagged in (1); location services: stop the app showing where you are (1).

practice.q: Explain **two** risks of using social networking sites.
practice.a: e.g. Information can be copied and spread widely (1) and can't be taken back once shared (1); strangers may not be who they say they are (1) and could be groomers (1); apps may share your location (1) so people can find you (1).

pages.spec: Recognise different forms of cyberbullying and trolling
pages.summary: Cyberbullying is using electronic devices to repeatedly and deliberately harm or harass someone. It can happen 24/7 and reach huge audiences. It includes threats, harassment, defamation, exclusion, identity theft and sharing private information. Trolling is deliberately posting upsetting comments.

blocks.text: **[[Cyberbullying]]** is when someone bullies others using **electronic devices**: social media, messaging services, mobile phones, tablets or gaming platforms. The behaviour is usually **repeated** and **deliberate**. It can be horrible for the people involved and hard for them to talk about.
How is cyberbullying different?

items: It can happen **24/7**, not just at school.
It follows you **into your home**, through your phone.
It can reach a **huge audience** instantly.
It is often **anonymous**, so the victim may not know who the bully is.
It can **escalate** quickly as other people join in, so the bullying comes from many people, not just a few.

blocks.text: Forms of cyberbullying

head: Form
What it looks like
rows: Messages that try to frighten someone.
Repeatedly sending offensive, threatening or unwanted messages.
Spreading untrue rumours that damage someone's reputation.
Deliberately leaving someone out of group chats or games.
Hacking into someone's account, or making a fake one, and posting as them.
Publicly posting or forwarding private information, photos or messages about someone.
blocks.caption: Forms of cyberbullying

blocks.text: Trolling

A **troll** is a person who causes upset online by starting arguments, upsetting people or posting **inflammatory** (deliberately angering) comments. **[[Trolling]]** is often aimed at disrupting a conversation and causing distress.
Catching the bullies

Keeping **evidence** of emails, posts and messages, and telling your parents, guardians, teachers and the police, helps track down bullies. Every device online has an **IP address**, which the police and CEOP can use to trace where bullying came from, even when it's 'anonymous'.

blocks.title: Worked example: is it cyberbullying?
blocks.context: In a class group chat, a few pupils keep posting a photo of Emma with mean comments, and remove her from the chat each time she's added back.
steps: Electronic device / platform? Yes: a group chat.
Repeated? Yes: it keeps happening.
Deliberate harm? Yes: mean comments, sharing her photo and excluding her.
blocks.answer: Yes: this is cyberbullying (sharing images + exclusion). Emma should keep screenshots and tell a trusted adult.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Cyberbullying = repeated, deliberate harm using electronic devices.
It can happen 24/7, reach big audiences and be anonymous.
Forms: threats, harassment, defamation, exclusion, identity theft, sharing private information.
Trolling = deliberately posting inflammatory comments to upset people.
Keep evidence: IP addresses can be used to trace bullies.

check.q: What is cyberbullying?
o: Repeatedly and deliberately harming someone using electronic devices
check.why: That's the definition.

check.q: Someone hacks a pupil's account and posts nasty messages as them. What form of cyberbullying is this?
check.why: Posting as someone else is impersonation.

check.q: What is a troll?
o: Someone who posts inflammatory comments to cause upset
check.why: Trolls deliberately start arguments and upset people.

check.q: How can 'anonymous' cyberbullies often be traced?
check.why: IP addresses can be traced.

practice.q: Define **cyberbullying**.
practice.a: Using electronic devices/social media/messaging (1) to repeatedly and deliberately harm, harass or upset someone (1).

practice.q: Explain **two** ways cyberbullying is different from face-to-face bullying.
practice.a: Any two: it can happen 24/7 / at home (1); it can reach a large audience instantly (1); it can be anonymous (1); it can escalate quickly with many people joining in (1).

pages.spec: Recognise the warning signs of online grooming and what counts as inappropriate content
pages.summary: Online groomers pretend to be someone they're not, build trust with gifts, compliments and shared interests, then try to move to private chat, get photos or arrange to meet. Inappropriate content is anything upsetting, adult, untrue or dangerous. Never meet an online contact.

blocks.text: Online grooming

It's easy to pretend to be someone else on the internet. **[[Online grooming]]** is when someone befriends a young person and builds an **emotional connection** with them, to lower their guard so they can exploit or abuse them.
How groomers work

items: They go to apps, games and social networks used by young people and **pretend to be one of them**, often using **fake profile pictures**.
They try to gain **trust** by pretending to have the **same interests**, **offering gifts** (like game currency) and saying **nice things**.
They try to move the chat from open platforms to **private messaging**.
Once they have the child's trust, they may steer the chat towards sexual topics or **ask for photos or videos**.
Some try to **set up a meeting**, or **blackmail** the child by threatening to share pictures with their family and friends.

blocks.text: Groomers are not always strangers. Sometimes they are people already met through family or activities, who use the internet to build a closer relationship. Some young people don't realise they're being groomed and think the person is their boyfriend or girlfriend.
**Crucial rule:** adults with bad intentions can easily fake a digital identity. **Never agree to meet** an online contact in person, and never send photos to someone you don't know.
Jenny's Story: what we learn

head: Question from the class discussion
The safe answer
rows: Would you pass a stranger's contact on to a friend?
No: you'd be putting your friend at risk too.
Would you let someone from a chatroom contact you by mobile, home phone or post?
No: never give your number or address to an online contact.
Would you meet up alone with someone you only know from the internet?
Never. Not alone, and not at all without a parent's knowledge.
If you were going to meet someone, would you tell someone?
You shouldn't meet, but a trusted adult must always know about any online contact who wants to.
Do you know how to save conversations?
Yes: take screenshots, as they can be used as evidence.
If you were worried about someone who contacted you, who would you tell?
A trusted adult: parent, guardian, teacher, form tutor, Head of Year or the school's Designated Teacher for Child Protection. You can also report to CEOP.
Would you send a photo to someone you don't know?
No: once sent, you lose control of it forever.
Best advice about chatting to strangers?
Don't share personal information, don't meet up, and tell a trusted adult if anything feels wrong.
blocks.caption: Jenny's Story discussion: answers

blocks.text: Inappropriate content

What counts as **[[inappropriate content]]** differs between people and depends on age and maturity. It includes information or images that are **upsetting**, material **meant for adults**, **inaccurate** information, or anything that might lead or tempt you into **dangerous or illegal behaviour**, for example: pornography; content with swearing; sites encouraging vandalism, crime, terrorism, racism, eating disorders or self-harm; violence or cruelty to people or animals; and unsupervised chats where nobody removes unsuitable comments.
If you see something online that upsets you, close it, don't share it, and tell a trusted adult. It is never your fault.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Grooming = building an emotional connection with a young person to exploit them.
Warning signs: fake profiles, gifts, lots of compliments, moving to private chat, asking for photos or to meet.
Groomers can be strangers or people you know.
Never meet an online contact and never send photos to people you don't know.
Inappropriate content is upsetting, adult, untrue or dangerous; tell an adult if you see it.

diagram.title: How grooming can progress
diagram.caption: Spotting the early stages helps you stop it.

nodes.label: Builds trust

nodes.detail: Asks to move to a private app, and to keep it secret.

nodes.label: Asks for more

nodes.label: Tell someone!
nodes.detail: At ANY stage: stop replying, keep evidence, tell a trusted adult, report to CEOP.

pages.spec: Explain what a digital footprint and a digital reputation are, and how quickly a post can spread
pages.summary: Your digital footprint is the often permanent trail left by everything you do online. Your digital reputation is how people see you because of it, and it can affect friendships and future jobs. A post can reach millions through friends of friends, so stop and THINK before you post.

blocks.text: Your digital footprint

Your **[[digital footprint]]** is *"the trail or history left behind by all your interactions using the internet, email, social media, texting, instant messaging and even on-demand TV."* It can often be **permanent**. Once something has been sent, you lose control over it.
Footprints in the sand: how far can a post spread?

blocks.title: Worked example: how many people could see your post?
blocks.context: You post a photo. You have 200 online friends, and each person has about 500 friends of their own.
steps: Your friends: **200** people can see it.
Friends of friends: 200 × 500 = **100,000** people.
Friends of friends of friends: 100,000 × 500 = **50,000,000** people.
blocks.answer: Up to 50 million people: that's over 25 times the population of Northern Ireland (about 1.9 million)!

blocks.text: Real numbers are smaller because friend groups overlap, but the point stands: a post can spread far beyond the people you meant it for.
Your digital reputation

Your **[[digital reputation]]** is defined by your **behaviour online** and by the **content you post** about yourself and others. Tagged photos, blog posts and social media interactions all shape how people see you, online and offline, now and in the future.
A poor digital reputation can affect your **friendships**, **relationships** and even your **job prospects**. Many employers and universities look people up online.
**THINK** before you post. Is it **T**rue? Is it **H**elpful? Is it **I**nspiring? Is it **N**ecessary? Is it **K**ind?
Some guidelines to remember

items: Never post pictures online that reveal personal details.
Never post personal information online.
Never post unacceptable comments online.
Keep your profile private.
Only accept real friends as your online friends.
Use an avatar as your profile picture.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Digital footprint = the trail left by everything you do online; often permanent.
One post can spread to millions through friends of friends.
Digital reputation = how others see you from your online behaviour and posts.
A poor reputation can affect friendships and job prospects, so stop and THINK before you post.

diagram.caption: Change the number of friends to see how many friends-of-friends-of-friends (each with 500 friends) could see a post.

What can a poor digital reputation affect?
check.why: It can affect your future.

check.q: What does the T in THINK stand for?
check.why: Is it True?

practice.a: A digital footprint is the trail/history of everything you do online (1); a digital reputation is how others see/judge you based on that behaviour and content (1).

practice.q: Explain why something you post online could affect you in the future.
practice.a: Posts can be permanent / copied and shared, so they can't be taken back (1); employers or others may see them later and judge you, affecting job prospects (1).
