pages.spec: Know exactly what to do if something online makes you uncomfortable, and nine tips for staying safe
pages.summary: If anything online makes you uncomfortable: don't delete it (it's evidence), don't reply, tell a trusted adult and report it to CEOP or Childline. Stay safe by using strong privacy settings, blocking and reporting, keeping personal details private and only friending people you know.

blocks.text: Feeling uncomfortable online? Do this
Saved messages and screenshots are [[evidence]]. Follow these four steps:

head: Step
Why
rows: Keep messages, images, emails and screenshots. They are **evidence** that police and school can use, for example to trace IP addresses, even if it goes to court.
Replying to bullies or trolls makes things worse and can make an investigation harder.
A parent, guardian, grandparent, form tutor, Head of Year, the school's Designated Teacher for Child Protection, or any teacher.
Use the **[[CEOP]]** reporting button (Child Exploitation and Online Protection) or contact **[[Childline]]** on **0800 1111**. You can also report on the app or game itself.
blocks.caption: What to do if something online worries you

blocks.text: If you think someone is in **immediate danger**, call **999**. CEOP is the place to report anyone trying to meet up with a child or acting in a sexual way online.
Nine tips for staying safe online

items: **Educate yourself** about what the social networks and apps you use actually do.
Set up **privacy settings** at the strongest level.
**Report** people and inappropriate conversations using the 'report' button, and always **keep a copy** as evidence.
**[[Block]]** or ignore people on social networks and games who make you feel uncomfortable.
**Never share personal details**: passwords, real name, address or school name.
**Friends should be people you know.** People online may not be who they say they are. Never agree to meet someone you don't know.
Know what you **should and shouldn't post** online.
Report directly to **CEOP** if someone is trying to meet up with a young person, or if someone is in immediate danger.
Remember that what you post **can't always be taken back**, and may already have been shared. This applies to **webcams** too.

blocks.title: Worked example: what should Niamh do?
blocks.context: Niamh keeps getting nasty anonymous messages on a social app saying nobody likes her.
steps: Don't delete: screenshot every message with the date and time.
Don't reply to the sender.
Block and report the account on the app.
Tell a trusted adult (a parent, her form tutor or Head of Year).
If it continues or she feels unsafe, the adult can involve the police; she can also talk to Childline on 0800 1111.
blocks.answer: Save, don't reply, block and report, tell an adult.

blocks.text: Don't just block and delete everything straight away. Save the evidence first!

blocks.title: Key points
items: Don't delete messages: they are evidence.
Don't reply to bullies or strangers.
Tell a trusted adult immediately.
Report to CEOP or call Childline on 0800 1111.
Use strong privacy settings, block and report, and never share personal details or meet online contacts.

pages.spec: Plan, organise and evaluate a team e-safety video project
pages.summary: In a team of three you plan, create and edit a video of up to 2 minutes promoting online safety. You share out roles, organise assets in folders, respect copyright, export the finished video and then use feedback to evaluate and improve it.

blocks.text: To finish the topic, you work in a **team of three** to plan, design, create and edit a video, **no longer than 2 minutes**, promoting **staying safe online**. It takes about three lessons, plus home learning.
Skills you'll need

head: Skill
What it means in the project
rows: Talking and listening so everyone knows the plan.
Files saved in the right folders, deadlines met.
Doing your fair share and helping others.
The video teaches real e-safety facts.
An original, eye-catching way to get the message across.
blocks.caption: Project skills

blocks.text: Team roles

head: Role
Who
Job
rows: Finds the facts and gathers suitable images.
Plans the storyboard and the look of the video.
Builds the project in a video editor (e.g. Clipchamp, Canva or MovieMaker).
Adds transitions, audio, effects and checks timing.
Keeps the team on track and files organised.
blocks.caption: Five roles shared between three people

blocks.text: Organising it all

You've already been file-management wizards, so now prove it! Create a folder called **E SAFETY** in your *Year 8 > ICT* folder, with subfolders **Images**, **Video Assets** and **Audio**. Give **everything** a meaningful name, and don't leave e-safety images in 'My Pictures'. If you record clips at home, bring them in on a USB stick or in Google Drive.

Respect **[[copyright]]**. Don't rip music or videos from YouTube with converter websites: it breaks YouTube's rules and can break copyright law, and those sites are full of pop-ups and malware. Use your own footage, **[[royalty-free]]** music and images, or school-approved libraries, and credit the owner.
Finishing and presenting

items: Check for transitions, audio, effects, timing, spelling, clarity and accurate information, and test that it plays.
**Export** the finished video in a suitable format such as **MP4** (or WMV), not the project file.
Name it with everyone's names, e.g. *ONLINE SAFETY VIDEO – BY MR BUTLER.mp4*.
Prepare notes for presenting it to the class. Classmates rate each video: two great things, one possible improvement, does it get the e-safety message across, and a score out of 10.

blocks.text: Feedback and evaluation

**[[Feedback]]** and **[[evaluation]]** matter because they let you judge the **progress** you've made, see your **strengths** and **areas for development**, recognise **what you've learnt** that you can use in future, and decide what **improvements** to make next time.

When you evaluate your video, take in comments from the class, your teacher, your group and your own view. Ask: Do all images, audio and video work? Is the message consistent? Is the look and feel consistent? Are the effects and transitions consistent? Is the narration good? A good evaluation is both **positive** and **critical**, e.g. *"I liked our colour scheme, but next time I'd keep all the text boxes the same style."*

blocks.title: Key points
items: Teams of three make a video (max 2 minutes) promoting online safety.
Roles: researcher, designer, creator, editor, organiser.
Organise assets in E SAFETY > Images, Video Assets, Audio, with meaningful names.
Respect copyright: use your own or royalty-free media and credit owners.
Export the final video (e.g. MP4) and use feedback to evaluate and improve.

check.why: No longer than 2 minutes.

o: The exported video, e.g. an MP4
check.why: Submit the exported video, not the project file.

o: It lets you judge progress and plan improvements
check.why: It shows strengths, weaknesses and next steps.

A set of rules that everyone must agree to before using the school's computers, to keep users, the network and data safe.
A punishment or consequence for breaking a rule, such as losing access to the network.
A computer on a network that a person sits at and uses, such as the PC in front of you in the ICT room.
A machine that stores and processes data by following a set of instructions called a program.
Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, text or pictures, before they are given meaning.
Two or more computers joined together so they can communicate and share things such as files and printers.
A massive worldwide network of computers linked together by physical hardware such as cables and routers.
A main computer that controls a network and provides services, such as storing everyone's files and sharing printers.
The network used by schools all across Northern Ireland; your school login and @c2ken.net email come from it.
Your unique username that tells the network who you are; nobody else has the same one.
A secret word or set of characters, known only to you, that proves you are who you say you are.
A password that is hard to guess or crack: at least 8 characters with capitals, lower case, numbers and symbols.
A single item of saved work or data, such as a document, photo or song, with a name and a file extension.
A container used to group and organise files (and other folders) so they are easy to find.
The letters after the dot at the end of a file name, such as .docx or .jpg, which show what type of file it is.
The top folder in a folder structure, which all the other folders are stored inside.
A spare copy of your files kept in a different place, so you can get them back if the originals are lost or damaged.
Short for electronic mail: a message sent from one computer to another over the internet.
The rules of good behaviour when sending emails and using the internet (from 'net' + 'etiquette').
The person who sends an email.
The person who receives an email.
The folder in your email where new messages you receive arrive.
A small face made from characters or a picture, such as :) , used to show feelings in a message.
Carbon copy: anyone in the CC box gets a copy of the email, and everyone can see they were copied in.
Blind carbon copy: anyone in the BCC box gets a copy of the email, but the other recipients cannot see they were sent it.
Sending an email back to the person who sent it to you; RE: appears before the subject.
Sending an email you received on to someone else; FW: appears before the subject.
A file, such as a document or photo, sent along with an email; shown by a paperclip icon.
The collection of millions of websites and web pages stored on computers connected to the internet; often called the WWW or the web.
Software used to view websites on the World Wide Web, such as Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Firefox or Safari.
A website, such as Google or Bing, that finds web pages matching the words you type in.
A sequence of clear, step-by-step instructions or rules followed to complete a task or solve a problem.
A harmful program that copies itself and is designed to damage files, steal information or make a computer unreliable.
A program that scans files, emails and USB sticks to find and remove viruses; it must be kept up to date.
Rules and actions that protect people from injury or illness, at school or at work.
A danger or risk: any source of potential damage, harm or bad health effects on something or someone.
Pain in the back, which can be caused by sitting in the same position for a long time or on a chair at the wrong height.
The way you hold your body when sitting or standing.
Tired, sore eyes caused by looking at a screen for a long time, made worse by glare and reflections.
Bright light reflecting off a screen, making it hard to see and tiring your eyes.
A screen or filter with a special coating that reduces reflections and glare.
Pain and damage, usually in the wrists, fingers or thumbs, caused by making the same movement again and again.
A soft support placed in front of a keyboard or mouse to keep your wrists straight and supported.
The science of designing safe and comfortable hardware and office furniture for humans.
Protecting computers, networks and data from damage, theft or people who should not have access.
An unauthorised user who gains access to a computer system or data by illegal means.
A risk to data that comes from someone inside an organisation, such as a careless or angry employee.

glossary.term: Health and Safety at Work Act
glossary.def: The 1974 law that sets out the duties employers and employees have to keep people safe at work, including when using ICT.
A legal responsibility to look after the safety and wellbeing of others, such as an employer's duty to employees.
A person who works for an employer and is paid by them.
The physical parts of a computer that you can touch, such as the keyboard, processor and monitor.
The programs and apps that run on a computer and tell the hardware what to do, such as Word, Chrome or a game.
Hardware that lets the user put data into a computer, such as a keyboard, mouse or microphone.
Hardware that lets the user receive information from a computer, such as a monitor, speakers or printer.
Where a computer keeps the data, programs and results it is using right now, for the short term; it is lost when the power is turned off.
Hardware that keeps files and installed software for the long term, even when the power is off, such as a hard disk drive or SSD.
The part of a computer that processes data by following the instructions it has been given; also called the CPU.
One of the parts that a computer is built from, such as the RAM or the power supply.
Central Processing Unit: the processor, the 'brain' of the computer that carries out instructions.
Random Access Memory: the computer's main memory, holding programs and data in use; it is wiped when the power goes off.
A storage device that stores data magnetically on spinning disks; it keeps data when the power is off.
The main circuit board that every other component plugs into, letting them communicate.
A component with its own processor (GPU) that creates the images shown on the monitor.
A metal block with fins, usually with a fan, that carries heat away from the CPU to stop it overheating.
Inside the computer's case, such as the RAM or motherboard.
Outside the computer's case and plugged in, such as a keyboard or monitor (also called a peripheral).
A cheap, credit-card-sized computer, designed in the UK, that you can plug into a TV and keyboard and use to learn programming.
A socket on a computer where you plug in a cable or device, such as a USB or HDMI port.
A computer designed mainly for playing games, such as a PlayStation, Xbox or Nintendo Switch.
A word made from the first letters of other words, such as RAM for Random Access Memory.
Universal Serial Bus: a standard connection used to connect devices, transfer data and supply power.
Read Only Memory: memory that keeps its contents when the power is off and holds the start-up instructions.
Solid State Drive: a fast storage device with no moving parts that stores data on memory chips.
Graphics Processing Unit: the processor that creates images and graphics.
High-Definition Multimedia Interface: a cable and port that carries high-quality video and sound to a TV or monitor.
Local Area Network: a network covering a small area such as a school or home.
A set of instructions carried out one after another, in the correct order.
A language such as Scratch, Python or C# used to write code that a computer can follow.
Instructions written in a programming language for a computer to carry out.
A diagram made of symbols and arrows that shows the steps of an algorithm in order.
A step in an algorithm that asks a question with a yes or no answer; drawn as a diamond in a flowchart.
Using a computer, rather than a person, to run a system automatically, such as traffic lights.
An input device that measures something in the real world, such as light, heat or movement.
The number system computers use, made of only two digits: 0 and 1.
A named location in memory that temporarily stores a value, such as a number or text, which can change while the program runs.
A set of instructions, written in code, that tells a computer what to do.
A pocket-sized programmable computer with 25 LEDs, two buttons and built-in sensors.
Light Emitting Diode: a small light; the micro:bit has 25 of them in a 5 × 5 grid.
A sensor that detects movement, such as shaking or tilting.
The kind of data a variable holds, such as integer, double, string, character or Boolean.
A data type for text: a sequence of characters, such as "Hello".
A data type for whole numbers, positive or negative, such as 7 or -3.
A data type that can only be true or false (or 1 or 0).
Using a condition (an IF statement) to decide whether a piece of code runs.
A test that is either true or false, such as score > 10.
Code that repeats; also called iteration.
A loop that repeats a set number of times, such as 'repeat 4 times' (a for loop).
A loop that keeps repeating while a condition is true, so we may not know how many times it will run (a while loop).
The safe and responsible use of technology, including the internet, phones, gaming devices and email.
Keeping control over your personal information and who can see it.
Someone who uses the internet safely, responsibly and respectfully towards others.
Information that could identify you or be used to find you, such as your full name, address, phone number or school.
Adding your exact location to a photo or post, often done automatically by your phone.
A picture or cartoon character used to represent you online instead of a real photo.
Options on an app or website that control who can see your posts and profile and who can contact you.
Playing games over the internet in real time with other people around the world.
Deliberately spoiling other players' game, for example by harassing them or cheating; a form of bullying.
Spending real money inside a game on extras such as skins, items or game currency.
Short for malicious software: any program designed to harm a computer or steal data, such as viruses, trojans, worms and spyware.
Malware disguised as genuine, useful software, such as a free game mod, that secretly lets attackers in.
Malware that spreads itself across a network from computer to computer without needing to attach to a file.
Software secretly installed to watch what you do and steal information such as passwords; a keylogger records every key you press.
Fake emails or messages pretending to be from a real organisation, such as a bank, to trick you into giving away personal details.
Secretly redirecting you from a real website to a fake copy to steal your login details.
The legal right of the creator to control who can copy, share or sell their work, such as music, films and software.
Using websites and apps such as Instagram, Snapchat or TikTok to share posts and messages and keep in touch with people.
Labelling a person in a photo or post, which links it to their profile.
A phone setting that lets apps know where you are using GPS.
Using electronic devices, such as phones, social media or gaming platforms, to repeatedly and deliberately harm or harass someone.
Deliberately posting offensive or provocative comments online to start arguments or upset people.
Spreading untrue things about someone that damage their reputation.
Pretending to be someone else, for example by hacking their account and posting as them.
When someone builds a friendship and emotional connection with a young person online in order to trick, exploit or abuse them.
Material that is upsetting, meant for adults, untrue, or that could lead you into dangerous or illegal behaviour.
The trail of information you leave behind from everything you do online; it is often permanent.
How others see you, based on your behaviour online and what you and others post about you.
Child Exploitation and Online Protection: part of the UK's National Crime Agency, where young people can report online abuse or worrying contact.
A free, confidential helpline for children and young people, on 0800 1111 or online.
Proof of what happened, such as saved messages or screenshots, that can be used by school or police.
To stop a person contacting you or seeing your profile on an app or game.
Looking back at your work to judge its strengths and weaknesses and decide how to improve it.
Comments from others, such as your teacher or classmates, about what is good in your work and what could be better.
Media (images, music, video) you are allowed to use without paying each time, as long as you follow its licence.
